1.pericope_label: Moses kept the flock of Jethro, and came to the mountain of God, even to Horeb

schools.summary: Henry divides the life into three forties — a prince in Pharaoh's court, a shepherd in Midian, a king in Jeshurun — and draws the lesson that it is sometimes long before God calls his servants out to the work he designed them for, since Moses was born to be Israel's deliverer and not a word is said of it to him until he is eighty. On the employment he is at his warmest: keeping sheep was a poor business for a man of Moses' parts and education, yet he rested satisfied in it and so learned meekness and contentment to a degree for which sacred writ celebrates him more than for all his learning. Those qualified for great employments must not think it strange to be confined to obscurity — let those who think themselves buried alive shine like lamps in their sepulchres, and wait till God's time comes for setting them on a candlestick. Henry adds that God encourages industry, since Satan loves to find us idle, and that retirement is a good friend to our communion with God: Moses saw more of God in a desert than ever in Pharaoh's court.

Calvin dwells on what the long training cost. The patience of the holy man is commended by his mere continuance in the work, and the inward conflict must have gone on, its question being why God should so long delay what he had so long ago determined; no temperance could protect even a robust body against the open air, the heat and cold and hunger — least of all a man bred to luxury, now lodging in huts and sheds. On the mountain Calvin makes Horeb and Sinai opposite sides of one mountain, the eastern properly Sinai and the western Horeb, and presses the point apologetically, since it answers those who have argued from the alternation of the names against the single authorship of the Pentateuch; he notes too that the mountain of God is used by anticipation, the place not yet having been consecrated by the giving of the Law. Gill finds a pattern rather than a discipline, noting that great persons have kept flocks and been called afterwards to the kingly office, as David was, and that the shepherding was an emblem of Moses' feeding and ruling Israel; on Jethro he leaves the question open but cites the heathen writer Demetrius, who says expressly that Jothor was a son of Raguel.

Keil and Delitzsch put the delay to positive account: while Israel groaned under the oppression, God had already prepared the way for their deliverance, having not merely chosen Moses as saviour of his people but trained him for the execution of his designs. Ellicott says the shepherding was the natural occupation of one who had thrown in his lot with the Midianites, and argues firmly that the word rendered father-in-law answers to the Latin affinis and is even applied to a husband, so that reading it as father-in-law produced the unlikely identification of Jethro with Reuel, whose son he more probably was, at once priest and sheikh of the tribe. On the mountain Ellicott makes Horeb the name of the entire region and Sinai the mass now called Jebel Musa.

Clarke reports that learned men do not agree on the term rendered father-in-law, which is translated son-in-law elsewhere; it seems a general word for a relative by marriage, and only the context can fix its sense. Since forty years had passed he thinks Reuel dead, Jethro his son and successor as prince and priest of Midian, and Zipporah Jethro's sister — in which case the word means brother-in-law. He says the mountain had two peaks, Sinai taking its name from the word for a bush. Wesley repeats Henry's division of the life into three forties and compresses the geography to two tops of one mountain.

2.pericope_label: The angel of the LORD appeared in a flame of fire out of the bush, and the bush was not consumed

schools.summary: Gill denies this was a created angel: he is afterwards called Jehovah and calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, which a creature would never do, so the Angel of God's presence and covenant is the eternal Word and Son of God. Calvin sets the question in a wider frame: God had to assume a visible form to be seen at all — not as he is in his essence but as the infirmity of the human mind could comprehend him — for whenever he appeared of old to the patriarchs he descended in some way from his majesty, revealing himself so far as their capacity would admit. On the turning aside Calvin will not let the curiosity be mere curiosity: Moses' mind was disposed to reverence by no rashness but by divine inspiration, and though unaccustomed to visions he perceived this was no unmeaning spectacle but held a mystery he must not neglect. What Calvin most wants noticed is his tractableness in turning aside to learn — for it often happens that God presents himself to us in vain, because we presumptuously reject so great a mercy; let us learn by Moses' example that as often as God invites us by any sign we give diligent heed, lest the proffered light be quenched by our own apathy.

Clarke argues from the titles — he is named Jehovah and has the most expressive attributes of the Godhead, yet he is truly a messenger, in whom was the name of God and in whom dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily; and who was this, Clarke asks, but Jesus, the Redeemer of mankind? He then widens the frame to comparative religion: fire was a significant emblem of the Deity not only among the Hebrews but among many other ancient nations, God went with Israel as a pillar of fire, and probably a flame in the holy of holies was the standing symbol of his presence — traditions of which, current through the east, Clarke thinks gave rise both to the general opinion that God appears in the likeness of fire and to the whole Zoroastrian system of fire-worship. Wesley reads the sign as addressed to Israel's present case: a flame to show that God was about to bring terror to his enemies and light and heat to his people, and a bush burning without being consumed as an emblem of the church then in bondage, burning in the brick-kilns yet not consumed, cast down but not destroyed. He hears Moses speaking as a man inquisitive and bold, determined to know the meaning of it if he could.

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew has an angel of Jehovah, but that in the next verse he is called both Jehovah and Elohim, whence it is concluded with reason that the Second Person of the Trinity appeared. He renders the plant the acacia, and argues that since that shrub is common in the Sinaitic region we can scarcely suppose a single tree growing alone is meant; the article is probably one of reference, so that the sense is the bush of which you have all heard. On the turning aside Ellicott finds evidence of authorship: it is a minute touch indicating that Moses is the writer, for he remembers that the bush did not grow on the track he was following but lay off it. Keil and Delitzsch identify the plant as the thorn-bush and observe that the symbolical sense of the vision — that it was a figurative representation of the nature and contents of the message about to be delivered — has long been admitted.

4.pericope_label: Put off thy shoes: I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob

schools.summary: Ellicott seizes on the Hebrew reading, when Jehovah saw, Elohim called, and treats it as decisive against the German theory of two authors of Exodus, one Jehovistic and one Elohistic: it is impossible to ascribe one clause of a sentence to one writer and the next to another. He notes that the doubling of the name marks extreme urgency, and that Orientals removed their sandals on entering any place to which respect was due — a temple, a palace, even the house of a great man — so that it is worthy of notice that God himself orders this mark of respect for the place his Presence has hallowed. On the divine self-naming Ellicott finds another weight in the wording: primarily it means the God whom the patriarchs worshipped, but the expression indicates their continued existence after death, since he can be the God only of existent things. On Moses hiding his face he compares Jacob's cry that the place was dreadful, and observes that though nothing was to be seen but an appearance as of material fire, the knowledge that God was there rendered the fire awful.

Calvin observes that this was no voiceless spectacle left to alarm the holy man, since instruction accompanied it — there would be no use in visions if the senses were merely kept in alarm — yet God claims authority by calling Moses twice by name, which makes its way into the depths of his heart, so that he listens as one cited before the tribunal of God. On the shoes he refuses the allegorists, dismissing their opinions as frivolous subtleties, and holds to the plain sense that by the bareness of his feet Moses' mind might be disposed to reverence. Calvin reads the naming of the patriarchs as demolition: by recalling the covenant God casts down all idols and confirms Moses in the true faith; and lest the lapse of time make what was handed down concerning Abraham seem obsolete, he asserts that his faithfulness still holds. Gill notes that the one called the Angel of the Lord is here plainly named Jehovah.

The command about the shoes sends Clarke through the ancient world: from this circumstance, he thinks, all the eastern nations came to worship barefooted, as Mohammedans, Brahmins and Parsees still do; the Jews were remarked for it in Juvenal's day; Pythagoras left it as a maxim to sacrifice and worship with the shoes off; and Tertullian describes the worshippers of Jupiter walking barefoot to pray for rain. On the fathers Clarke notes that the singular is quoted in the plural by Stephen, a reading the Samaritan and Coptic confirm, and presses the three names further — Abraham father of the Ishmaelites, Isaac of the Edomites as well as the Israelites, Jacob of the twelve patriarchs — concluding that Arabs and Turks, Edomites and scattered Jews alike are heirs of this primitive covenant, and their gathering in with the fullness of the Gentiles may be confidently expected. Wesley draws out how narrowly it turned: had Moses neglected the sight, it is likely God would have departed and said nothing. Divine calls are effectual when the Spirit makes them particular — the Word calls, Ho, every one; the Spirit, applying it, calls, Ho, such a one. He translates the gesture, saying that putting off the shoe was then what putting off the hat is now, and takes thy father strictly, of Amram, against the collective reading.

7.pericope_label: I have surely seen the affliction of my people, and am come down to deliver them

schools.summary: Gill takes the doubled Hebrew verb to mean not merely certainty but a clear and full sight, carrying sympathy with it and a settled determination to deliver — God had long observed their affliction and was afflicted with them in it. He insists the coming down must be understood consistently with the omnipresence of God, who cannot strictly be said to remove from place to place; such language is used when he gives some eminent display of his power or goodness, and Christ in our nature likewise came down to save his spiritual Israel. Calvin says God is said to descend when he actually puts forth his power and shows himself near, so that Israel would plainly find his help at hand; he reads the breadth of the promised land against their present state, since Goshen was fertile and convenient but scarcely afforded room for their increasing multitude, and there they were kept shut in like slaves in a house of bondage. Calvin also notes the order of the address, that God furnishes his servant with promises before laying on any command — the best encouragement to duty being to make a doubting man sure of good success; and though God sometimes withholds hope to try obedience, more often he cuts off hesitation by promising success.

Henry counts three things God took notice of. Their sorrows first — they were probably not permitted to lay their grievances before Pharaoh, nor scarcely durst complain to one another, but God observed their tears, for even the secret sorrows of his people are known to him. Then their cry, since God is not deaf. Then the tyranny of their persecutors. And Henry marks the timing: after forty years of bondage and banishment, when both they and Moses might well have despaired, God came — for he often comes for the salvation of his people when they have done looking for him.

Ellicott sharpens the grammar against the usual reading, holding that the idiom implies not so much certainty as continued looking; he notes too that the word for taskmasters differs from the one used earlier and carries cruel usage, and calls the coming down a condescension to human infirmity, which conceives all things under the limitations of time and space — observing that not even the Jews understood it literally, as Solomon's prayer at the temple shows. Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the two adjectives applied to the land — good for its great fertility, broad in deliberate contrast with the confinement the Israelites suffered in Egypt — and treat the phrase about milk and honey as a proverbial description of the fertility and loveliness of Canaan.

Clarke explains the proverb about milk and honey: the country was excellent for pasturage, abounding in wholesome herbage and flowers from which the bees collected wild honey, and though cultivation is now neglected there through bad government, it still yields both. He adds that the figure is drawn from a breast producing copious streams of milk, and finds it in Homer, who calls Argos the breast of the country, and in Virgil's line that the land which first produced you shall receive you again into its joyous bosom. Wesley agrees the idiom of coming down marks something extraordinary, and turns it forward: this deliverance was typical of our redemption, in which the eternal Word did indeed come down from heaven to deliver us. He closes on the man chosen — the same hand that fetched a shepherd out of a desert to plant the Jewish church afterwards fetched fishermen from their ships to plant the Christian church, that the excellency of the power might be of God.

11.pericope_label: Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh? Certainly I will be with thee

schools.summary: Gill measures the two parties: on one side a poor shepherd, an exile unknown to Pharaoh; on the other a great king with forces enough to prevent Israel's departure — there had been a time when Moses made a figure in that court as the king's daughter's adopted son, but it was now otherwise. Calvin refuses to read the hesitation as a failure of nerve and reverses the usual valuation: it is not disobedience but the excuse of modesty, which he judges not merely free from blame but worthy of praise, Moses simply wondering that another was not chosen since God has thousands of beings at command. As for the earlier boldness in killing the Egyptian, Calvin will not put the change down to age: the fault lay the other way, that Moses had advanced hastily at first without weighing his own powers or the greatness of the undertaking — and such precipitation, however praiseworthy it looks, often fails in mid course. On the answer Calvin marks the economy: God sets his ready help alone against everything feared, as much as to say that it matters nothing who Moses is, provided God is his leader; from which he concludes that God is never regarded with due honour unless, contented with his assistance alone, we seek no ground of confidence apart from him.

Henry divides the plea in two — Moses thinks he wants courage, and so cannot go to Pharaoh with a demand that might cost the demandant his head; and thinks he wants skill, and so cannot bring out a people unarmed, dispirited and utterly unable to help themselves. Yet Henry insists he was incomparably the fittest man living for the work, eminent for learning, wisdom, valour, faith and holiness, and draws the rule that the more fit a person is for service, commonly the less opinion he has of himself. On the change from the man who once killed an Egyptian, Henry treats it as a fluctuation of temper — Moses had formerly been courageous, but now his heart failed him, for good men are not always alike bold and zealous.

Ellicott makes it a pattern: the men most fit for great missions are apt to deem themselves unfit, as Jeremiah pleaded that he was a child, and Ambrose fought to escape being made bishop of Milan. In Moses' case he grants real disqualifications alongside the obvious fitness: forty years of exile had at once unfitted him for a court and made him a stranger to his brethren, and want of eloquence seemed fatal in a man who must work chiefly by persuasion. On the reply Ellicott notices that it is not addressed to the thing said but to the thing meant — Moses meant to urge that he was unfit; God answers, not unfit, since I will be with thee. He takes the worship on the mountain to be precisely the sign, since it accords with the divine economy to give men tokens which lie in the future and appeal to faith only. Keil and Delitzsch reach Calvin's conclusion in a phrase: Moses had once offered himself of his own accord as deliverer and judge, but had now learned humility in the school of Midian.

Clarke adds that Moses was so satisfied the work lay beyond his power that he is astonished God should appoint him — and thinks him right, since had the deliverance not come by supernatural means their escape would have been impossible. Against Ellicott he holds that the worship on the mountain was not the sign at all, but a further disclosure that they should take this mountain in their way, with perhaps a prophetic allusion to the law given there; the assurance of God's presence, he says, means that the great event shall not be left to Moses' wisdom and power. Wesley says it plainly: those weak in themselves may do wonders being strong in the Lord, and God's presence answers all objections.

13.pericope_label: What is his name? And God said, I AM THAT I AM

schools.summary: Clarke explains the question by Egypt, asking whether it does not suppose an idolatrous notion of the Supreme Being among a people who had drunk deep of the Egyptian superstitions. On the Name he assembles the versions — the Vulgate's I am who am, the Arabic's the Eternal, who passes not away, the Targums' he who spake, and the world was — before admitting frankly that it is difficult to put a meaning on the words, though they seem intended to mark the eternity and self-existence of God. He finds the promise about the memorial literally fulfilled, since even the heathens knew the name and formed from it their Jao, Jeve and Jove. Wesley sees two names given rather than one: the first speaks what God is in himself — self-existent, depending on no other and so all-sufficient, the inexhaustible fountain of being and bliss; eternal and unchangeable; faithful to all his promises — while the second speaks what he is to his people, given, Wesley observes shrewdly, lest the first should puzzle them.

Ellicott notes that in Egypt, and wherever polytheism prevailed, every god had a name as a matter of course, whereas among the Israelites God had been known only by titles — the Lofty One, the Powerful, the Existent — none yet hardened into a proper name, so that Moses imagines the people may have grown so far Egyptianised as to want more. On the Name itself he makes the difficulty the point rather than a defect: it is generally assumed the phrase is God's full name, but perhaps it is rather a deep and mysterious statement of his nature, meaning that his nature cannot be declared in words nor conceived by human thought, his whole inscrutable nature being implied in his existing at all. He traces the later history too: the first-person form is here turned into the third with no change of meaning, and becomes the predominant name through the Old Testament; it does not occur in the New, where Lord takes its place, though an equivalent appears in John's vision. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the Egyptian explanation outright: the supposition owes nothing to the Egyptian analogy, since the name by which God revealed himself to the fathers cannot have vanished entirely from the people's memory.

Calvin argues against the Egyptian explanation from Moses' side: who can think the faith of the holy prophet so obliterated that he had forgotten the God he devoutly served? His concession is that the faith of both had grown faint and rusty, the brightness of the ancient religion still shining, but only in small sparks. On the Name he observes that the Hebrew verb is future, I will be what I will be, yet carries the force of the present with the added sense of perpetual duration; and he marks a deliberate irregularity, the same verb being used as a noun in the first person and joined to a third-person verb, so that our minds may be filled with admiration whenever his incomprehensible essence is mentioned. He reads the second name as a boundary line: God takes again the name drawn from his covenant, so that Israel may know they are not deceiving themselves in an uncertain God; and as soldiers assemble round their standard, he commands them to look back on the grace of their adoption, confining them within those limits that they may not wander in search of God. Gill takes the Name for the real being of God, his self-existence, his being the Being of beings, and his constancy in fulfilling promises, since it takes in all time: I am what I have been, and shall be what I am.

16.pericope_label: Go, and gather the elders of Israel together: I have surely visited you

schools.summary: Gill denies that the word means all the ancient men, or the judges — no such office appears among them in Egypt, he says, until they came into Canaan — and takes it of the heads of tribes or families; he glosses the following phrase as what God had resolved within himself and now declared. Calvin explains why the message goes to the elders first: it was not easy either to gather the whole people into one place or for a commission to be heard by so great a multitude, so Moses is to begin with them, that they may by their authority arouse the body of the people to a good hope. There was practical necessity in it too, since the dismissal had to be sought from the king in the name of all and every mind prepared for departure. Calvin adds that the naming of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob is not idle: the vision would otherwise have been hardly credible, and it is made credible by resting on the ancient covenant deposited with them. From the following words he draws a further lesson — that God determines in his secret counsel what he will do, so we must restrain desires which otherwise press forward too fast, not because he needs time to deliberate, but that we may learn to depend on his providence — and he notes that the nations are enumerated, and the land called one flowing with milk and honey, to draw them out, particularly lest its barrenness should alarm a people whose fathers had been driven from it by famine.

Henry states the messenger's duty in a sentence: what ministers have received of the Lord they must deliver to his people, keeping back nothing that is profitable. He then lays the weight of the passage on two words — I have said, that is enough to satisfy them; has he spoken, and will he not make it good? With us saying and doing are two things, but they are not so with God, for he is in one mind and who can turn him; he has said it, and all the world cannot gainsay it. Henry also marks the promise that the elders will listen, hearing in it both a prophecy and its cause: they shall hearken and not thrust thee away as they did forty years ago, since he who inclines the heart and opens the ear could say so beforehand, having determined to make them willing in the day of his power.

Keil and Delitzsch call the elders the representatives of the nation, the heads of families, households and tribes, whom Moses was to inform first of all. Ellicott takes the opposite view from Clarke on whether an enslaved people kept any government of its own: the word means not the old men generally but the rulers, and Rosenmüller reasonably concludes from the direction given here that the Hebrews enjoyed some internal organisation and native government even under the oppression. Ellicott also hears in the following words a reference back to the promise once made to Abraham.

Clarke thinks it not likely the Hebrews were permitted any regular government at this time, though he has no doubt they had one in Joseph's day, the elders of each tribe forming a kind of court of magistrates before which actions were tried. He notices that the phrase about visiting them is an exact fulfilment of Joseph's dying prediction that God would surely visit them, and in the very same words.

18.pericope_label: Let us go three days' journey: I am sure the king of Egypt will not let you go

schools.summary: Clarke takes the three days' journey as plain geography — Mount Sinai is evidently meant, about three days' journey from Goshen by the shortest way — and observes that distances were then computed by the time needed to cross them, as still happens where there are no regular roads. On the hardest words in the passage he says the received rendering yields a palpable contradiction, since the book itself declares that the king did let them go, and by a mighty hand; he therefore takes the Hebrew negative in the sense of unless or except, which he says it sometimes bears, noting that Becke's Bible of 1549 so translated it and the Vulgate and the Greek understood it so — the meaning being that Pharaoh, who profits much by the servitude, will not let them go till he sees the hand stretched out. Wesley puts the forewarning as a rule of providence: God sends his messengers to those whose obstinacy he foresees, that it may appear he would have them turn and live.

Ellicott finds a religious necessity behind the distance, arising from that remarkable peculiarity of the Egyptian religion, the worship of animals: cows, or at any rate white cows, were sacred throughout Egypt, so that a sacrifice the Hebrews thought ordinary would be an outrage where they stood. He notes too that Pharaoh would readily comprehend the message, understanding that the Hebrews, being of a different race, had a God of their own who might give intimations of his will — as the Egyptian kings supposed their own gods did. On the disputed clause Ellicott takes it in the contrary sense to Clarke, rendering it not even under a mighty hand: Pharaoh, though chastised by that hand, will not voluntarily permit their departure. He also corrects the opening verb, since the Hebrew is I know, better suiting a speaker to whom the future is as certain as the past; and he closes on the promise that follows — hands are stretched out to help and save, and God promises here more than before, showing how he will be with Moses by lending miraculous aid.

Calvin questions the usual rendering of the promise about the elders: the literal words are they shall hearken to thy voice, which many take as a promise of obedience, but he thinks after they shall have heard thy voice more consonant — God first commands them through Moses, and only then do they go with him to Pharaoh. He also weighs the word for God's meeting with them, which means he presented himself voluntarily: they had cried out often enough before, but this was an unlooked-for approach on his side. On the forewarning of Pharaoh's refusal Calvin observes that interpreters differ, and turns to its purpose: God arms his people lest a repulse at the first onset send them home in despair — a stubbornness discovered unexpectedly would have discouraged them far more, though it was hard to be told their errand would be vain and that they might as well address the trunk of a tree. And if the useless labour and the ridicule seem absurd, Calvin answers that it was for example and for the setting forth of God's glory, that the king, civilly applied to, should betray his own impious perversity; nothing being juster than that what he unjustly refused should be extorted from him against his will. Gill reads the promise as an assurance that the elders would credit the commission and not reject Moses as some had before.

21.pericope_label: Ye shall not go empty: every woman shall ask jewels of silver and of gold

schools.summary: Calvin sees an inducement: by this exercise of his bounty God encourages them to strive more heartily, promising not only liberty but abundance; and since it was hard to believe their bitterest enemies would turn so liberal, God reminds them that it lies in his power to turn men's hearts wherever he will — he will make these wolves of Egypt become like lambs, so that those who used to bite and devour shall supply them with the very wool off their backs. From this he draws a wide doctrine: when men rage against us it is not contrary to God's design, since he could quiet them in a moment, and our alarm is the just reward of our unbelief in not reposing on his providence. On the moral difficulty of the spoiling, Calvin grants their labour deserved recompense but thinks that too small a ground. Those who find this little in accordance with God's justice, he says, reflect little how widely that justice extends: God does defend every man's rights and prohibit theft, but let us ask what any man's property is. Who can boast that he has anything except what God gave, on condition that each hold what God pleases, he being free to take it away at any moment? Should the Egyptians complain of injury, they would be arguing against God for transferring his own free gifts. This does not make God lawless: his will being the most certain rule of equity, whatever he does must be right. Gill sets the favour just before the departure, and says the Israelites spoiled the Egyptians very justly, for the hard service they had been put to, this being no more than the wages due.

Clarke states flatly that borrow is wrong, the Hebrew meaning simply to ask or demand, and calls it a gross mistake into which scarcely any version ancient or modern has fallen except our own: the Greek has she shall ask and the Vulgate she shall demand, while the common English version is almost the sole transgressor, copying Becke's Bible of 1549, whereas the Geneva Bible rightly renders it aske. He is sharpest about what the bad translation cost: it has given countenance to infidelity, whose abettors say Moses represents God as ordering them to borrow under pretence of returning, when he meant them to march off with the booty — whereas if accounts were fairly balanced Egypt would still be in arrears. Clarke adds that while the oppression lasted they could accumulate no property, their gains going to their oppressors. Wesley disposes of the word in a parenthesis: every woman shall ask, not borrow; and he says God has many ways of balancing accounts between the injured and the injurious.

Ellicott settles the question from the narrative rather than the lexicon: there was no pretence of borrowing, since the jewels were not asked for until the moment of departure, when the Israelites were being thrust out and the people urgent on them to be gone, neither expecting nor wishing to see them again. Asking for presents, he adds, is a common practice in the East. He closes on the detail: Egyptian men of that period wore gold and silver ornaments almost as freely as the women, and to spoil them means it should be as if Israel had conquered them.
